full_judgment:
2.1 Facts, relevant for the disposal of the appeals, in short, are that in response to international tenders floated by the appellant, being Tender Inquiry Nos. PUR-3.1865/2007-2008 dated 11-9-2007, PUR-3.1863/2007-2008 dated 18-6-2007 PUR-3.1862/2007-2008 dated 18-6-2007, PUR-3.1883/2007-2008 dated 20-9-2607 and PUR-3.1847/2006-2007 dated 26-6-2007, to procure fertilizers, the respondent participated in the said tenders and became successful bidder. Accordingly, the bids of the respondent were accepted by the appellant. Thereupon, the respondent submitted performance bank guarantees, being Bank Guarantee Nos. 226/2007, 227/2007, 228/2007, all dated 31-10-2007, Bank guarantee Nos. 176/2007 and 175/2007, both dated 17-9-2007, Bank guarantee No. 271/2007 dated 6-12-2007 and Bank guarantee No. 162/2007 dated 6-9-2007, along with other necessary papers, in terms of the said acceptance letters. Thereupon, the appellant issued purchase orders, being Ref. Nos. PUR-3.1865/2007-2008/CT-245(F)3273 dated 12-11-2007, PUR-3.1863/2007-2008/ CT230(F) 2685 dated 24-9-2007, PUR-3.1862/2007- 2008/CT229(F)2648 dated 24-9-2007, PUR-3.1883/2007-2008/ CT-259(F)3809 dated 17-12-2007 and PUR-3.1847/2007-2008/ CT233(F) 2547 dated. 13-9-2007. Accordingly, the respondent opened LC for importation of the said fertilizers. Thereafter, the delivery was delayed on two occasions due to the extreme vessel crises in China and extensions of time were given by the appellant. The respondent further prayed for extension of time, but the appellant (procuring entity) cancelled the purchase orders on 17-2-2008 and forfeited the bank guarantees furnished by the respondent. Being aggrieved by such action of the appellant (procuring entity), the respondent filed five title suits before the learned District Judge, Dhaka and obtained ad-interim orders of status-quo in respect of the encashment of the said bank guarantees. However, the learned District Judge, Dhaka, subsequently, directed the parties to settle the disputes through arbitration in accordance with the arbitration clause as contained in the agreements between the parties. The parties then took initiative to settle the disputes through arbitration and, accordingly, appointed their respective arbitrators, who then appointed the third arbitrator as Chairman. The Arbitration Tribunal then, after hearing the claimant (respondent) and the second party (appellant), delivered the awards by majority opinion on 21-7-2011 in respect of the aforementioned five purchase orders and, thereby, allowed the claims of the claimant (respondent). By the awards, the Tribunal directed the appellant to return/release the said bank guarantees within 2 (two) months from date of the receipt of the award, in default the respondent would be entitled to release the said amounts with interest @ 10% per annum. Being aggrieved by these awards, the appellant (procuring entity) filed the aforementioned five miscellaneous cases before the Court of District Court, Dhaka under section 42(1) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 seeking cancellation of the said awards. Thereupon, the learned District Judge, Dhaka, after hearing the parties, dismissed the said miscellaneous cases on contest vide impugned judgment and orders dated 30-3-2015 and, thereby, refused to cancel the said awards. Being aggrieved by such dismissals, the procuring entity preferred these appeals under section 48 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. The appeals are contested by the respondent (supplier) through learned advocate Mr Md Rashed Khan. 

 3.3 As against above submissions, Mr Md Rashed Khan, learned advocate appearing for the respondent-supplier, submits that in view of the provisions under sections 42 and 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, the jurisdiction of the learned District Judge in examining the propriety of an award delivered by the Arbitration Tribunal is very limited and the learned District Judge can only interfere into such award if the same is hit by the mischiefs as provided by sub-clauses M and Of) of sub-section (1) of section 43. According to him, learned District Judge, sitting under sections 42 and 43 of the said Act, cannot act as an appellate Court and it cannot set-aside an award on merit unless it is found that the award is absurd and against the public policy of the country. By referring to a judgment of our Appellate Division in Saudi Arabian Airlines vs Saudi Bangladesh, 73 DLR (AD) 277, learned advocate for the respondent submits that in this decision the Appellate Division elaborately discussed the issue of public policy wherein it was held that an award could be contrary to public policy if the same was found to be 'patent illegal' and that such illegality must go to the root of the matter. Therefore, according to him, since there is nothing in the awards in question which may be termed as `patent illegality', the same cannot be termed as against the public policy of the country. Accordingly, he submits that this Court has got nothing to interfere into the impugned judgment and orders passed by the Court below. 

 4.7 Therefore, it appears from the above observation of the Tribunal that the Tribunal has addressed the said issue of time being essence of the contract in detail and has expressed its view on the same by holding that the supplier did not willfully neglect to make shipment and that since the buyer had given extensions of time twice, it could have given further extension as the supplier did have the intention to supply the goods. It was further addressed by the Tribunal that the agre( II-lent between the parties had a 'force majeure' clause under Clause No. 23.01 and, as per the said Clause, the supplier was entitled not to supply because of intervening acts beyond his control. It is true that if the learned District Judge sits on these awards as an appellate Court, it may have the option to take a different view on the same. But because of such option, the awards cannot be cancelled in view of the provisions under section 43 of the said Act, and this position has been reaffirmed by our Appellate Division in the above referred case of Saudi Arabian Airlines vs Saudi Bangladesh, 73 DLR (AD) 277. Therefore, it appears that learned District Judge concerned in fact did not have any option but to hold that such awards could not be cancelled as because the same did not suffer from the mischiefs as provided by section 43 of the said Act. Therefore, we are of the view that on this point, the judgment of the learned District Judge cannot be interfered with.
